theory_title: What the market is paying for a rupee of profit
theory_content: P/E is price divided by earnings per share. A P/E of 25 means paying ₹25 for every ₹1 of annual profit. It is only meaningful against something: the company’s own history, its peers, or the market. A high P/E is not automatically expensive — it reflects expected growth — and a low one is not automatically cheap, because it often reflects expected decline.

theory_title: A company is worth the cash it will produce
theory_content: A DCF estimates the future free cash flows of a business and discounts them back to today at a rate reflecting their risk. The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are not. Small changes to the growth rate or discount rate swing the answer enormously, which is why a DCF is best used to ask what the current price already assumes rather than to produce a target.

theory_title: How efficiently the business uses its capital
theory_content: ROE is net profit divided by shareholders’ equity. A business earning 25% on equity compounds shareholder capital far faster than one earning 8%, and can fund its own growth without raising money. Check how it is achieved: ROE inflated by heavy debt is a different and more fragile thing than ROE from high margins.

theory_title: The gap between value and price
theory_content: Estimates are wrong, so buy only when the price is meaningfully below your estimate of value — the difference absorbs the error. This is the practical answer to the fragility of DCF: you do not need to be precisely right if you have bought with enough room to be somewhat wrong.
